absent: Common event collection helper behaviour and timeout semantics beyond delegation
Compatibility signal mask installation and restoration mechanics
Pseudo filesystem superblock teardown and mount lifetime rules
Anonymous security initialization policy and failure causes
Pseudo file allocation and descriptor installation internals
Identity mapping translation and namespace capability evaluation
Version increment protocol and change cookie consumption
Timestamp truncation rules and clock source guarantees

Shared versus secure inode selection policy outside the routed callers
Locking context for attribute preparation and commitment callers

findings.text: Two compatibility entry points expose timed event collection with an optional caller timeout and an optional compatibility signal description. One accepts a legacy narrow timeout representation while the other accepts a wide native representation. Both validate user memory before waiting and delegate collection to a shared helper. The observable contract is identical apart from timeout decoding.

Waits through the compatibility event entry points run under a temporarily installed compatibility signal mask. The prior mask is conditionally restored based on whether a signal became pending during the wait. A wait that was interrupted but collected no events reports ERESTARTNOHAND rather than success.

Invalid user addresses for timeout or compatibility signal description cause the compatibility event waits to fail with EFAULT before any wait occurs. A rejected signal mask installation likewise aborts the operation and propagates its status.

The anonymous inode layer exports constructors for unnamed files and descriptors with caller supplied name operations private data and flags. Variants cover shared inode reuse versus fresh secure inode creation with optional security context, plus a mode augmenting file variant and descriptor installing wrappers. Secure creation binds the new inode to the caller context.

Anonymous inode behaviour is defined by an inode operations table that provides attribute query and attribute update handlers. The query handler supplies generic attributes with type information removed. The update handler unconditionally refuses modification.

Anonymous inode filesystem identity comprises dentry operations with a dynamic name handler, a context initializer establishing pseudo filesystem state with a dedicated magic value and the dentry operations, and a filesystem type record linking a fixed name with context initialization and superblock teardown.

Attribute queries on anonymous inodes reflect the underlying inode through generic filling under a neutral identity mapping, then clear file type bits from the reported mode while preserving permission bits. The operation always reports success.
Attribute updates on anonymous inodes are never applied and always report EOPNOTSUPP.

The anonymous inode mount and its shared inode reside in write protected storage after early initialization. Early initialization mounts the pseudo filesystem and allocates the shared inode, halting the system if either step fails, and assigns the anonymous inode operations to the shared inode.

Anonymous file acquisition progresses from owner reference accounting through inode sourcing toward pseudo file instantiation. Inode sourcing either creates a fresh secure inode bound to a name and context or reuses the shared inode with an additional reference. Instantiation filters caller flags to access mode and nonblocking behaviour, wires the inode mapping and private data, and on any failure releases the inode reference and owner reference.

Descriptor constructors wrap the file acquisition outcome together with caller descriptor flags through a helper that prepares and installs a descriptor. Success yields an installed descriptor while acquisition failure propagates as an error status.

Anonymous dentry names are rendered by formatting a fixed prefix together with the dentry name into the tail of the supplied buffer. Results exceeding NAME_MAX or the buffer capacity are rejected with ENAMETOOLONG.

Generic attribute filling populates device identity, inode number, mode, link count, mapped owner identities, device number for special files, size, access time, block size derived from block bits, and block count. Owner translation flows from inode stored identities through the supplied identity mapping using the filesystem user namespace.

Change and modification time reporting selects between multigrain and regular storage. The multigrain path consults the request mask and may suppress both times when neither was requested, while the regular path reports stored stamps. Change cookie reporting additionally requires both a request flag and filesystem version support.

Size and timestamp reads use concurrency safe accessors without requiring caller locking. Size handling adapts to word size and configuration using sequence protection, preemption control, or ordered loads. Timestamp component reads use single access semantics, with change time nanosecond reads masking a query marker.

Version queries observe a raw version word and ensure a queried marker becomes set through a compare exchange retry loop with ordering guarantees. The reported value is the stored version with marker bits removed.

Multigrain change time observation and delegation coordinate through atomics on the nanosecond field. Observation records a queried marker exactly once and reports the stamp without the marker. Delegation attempts an atomic nanosecond exchange with a single retry when the only change was concurrent marking, otherwise adopting the winning stamp.

Attribute preparation first enforces size constraints that force cannot override, including denial of size changes on verity protected inodes. Ownership, group, mode and timestamp changes each require dedicated authorization, with group management stripping an unsupported group inheritance bit. Forced updates skip authorization checks but still invoke privilege revocation handling when requested.

Ownership change authorization succeeds for a self owned inode keeping the same owner, for holders of ownership alteration privilege relative to the inode, or for unmapped owners when the filesystem namespace grants that privilege. Group change authorization additionally allows the file owner to select the current group or any group containing the caller.

Size validation rejects negative targets. Growth is bounded by the file size resource limit with signal delivery on excess and by the filesystem maximum. Shrinkage of active swap storage is rejected as busy. Resource and maximum excess share a too large failure status.

Set user identity removal is always requested when present, while set group identity removal depends on group execute permission and on group membership or privilege. The combined removal request applies only to regular files when the caller lacks the relevant privilege.

Attribute commitment updates owner and group conditionally through identity mapping translation and refreshes mode with group inheritance protection. Time commitment follows a multigrain path handling explicit versus implied stamps or a legacy path applying supplied stamps, with explicit change time routed through delegation.

Mode ownership group and timestamp setting are denied on immutable or append restricted inodes. Timestamp touching on immutable inodes is likewise denied, and touching by a non owner requires write authorization on the inode.

Attribute and size operations carry distinct failure modes including immutable or append denial, authorization failure, faulty size with signal, busy swap truncation, and verity protection. Size checks precede authorization and forced updates do not bypass size or revocation failures.

Delegated change time update discards proposals not newer than the current stamp, limits future proposals to the current clock, and normalizes through timestamp truncation. Identical proposals leave state unchanged. Competing updates resolve by atomic exchange, preserving a concurrent fresher stamp over the delegated proposal.

The anonymous inode filesystem is identified by a fixed registration name and a dedicated filesystem magic established during context initialization. These values constitute the stable identity used to recognize and mount the pseudo filesystem.

Early initialization establishes the anonymous inode mount and its shared inode as system wide resources and assigns the anonymous inode operations. Failure at either step halts initialization rather than returning a degraded state.

Anonymous file creation fails cleanly on owner reference failure, secure inode allocation or security initialization failure, missing shared inode, pseudo file allocation failure, and overlong rendered names. Mount and shared inode initialization failures are fatal during early boot.
